lines.text: This time, the rest of the cutting kit: chisels, the hammer, and the plane, each one beside its Western cousin.

lines.text: Japanese chisels, nomi, come in two families. Tataki-nomi are struck with a hammer. Tsuki-nomi are pushed by hand, with no hammer.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress. Say the Japanese words 'nomi', 'tataki' and 'tsuki' with short, crisp, even syllables: no long vowels at all.
lines.tts: Japanese chisels, nomi, come in two families. Tataki nomi are struck with a hammer. Tsuki nomi are pushed by hand, with no hammer.

lines.text: A struck chisel has an iron hoop fitted around the end of its handle. This hoop is called the katsura.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: A struck chisel has an iron hoop fitted around the end of its handle. This hoop is called the kah-tsoo-rah.

lines.text: The general bench chisel, struck with a hammer, is the oire-nomi. You'll also see it read oiire, or written ōire. For deep mortises there is the mukōmachi-nomi, with a thick blade.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The general bench chisel, struck with a hammer, is the oh-ee-reh nomi. You'll also see it read oh-ee-ee-reh, or written oh-oh-ee-reh. For deep mortises there is the moo-koh-mah-chee nomi, with a thick blade.

lines.text: Now look at the blade itself. A woodworking chisel is bevelled on one side only. And it's made of two layers: a thin layer of hard steel, hagane, forge-welded to a thicker body of softer iron, jigane. The softer iron supports the brittle steel and absorbs shock, so the steel doesn't break. One Japanese blade maker puts it simply: foreign blades are usually one piece of steel; Japanese blades are laminated.

lines.text: The back of the blade has a shallow hollow, the urasuki. It makes the back easier to flatten. The hollow is in the back, not the bevel: the chisel is not hollow-ground.

lines.text: The hammer is the gennō. One face is flat; the other is slightly domed.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The hammer is the gen-noh. One face is flat; the other is slightly domed.

lines.text: Driving a nail, you strike with the flat face, then give the last blows with the domed face, so the surface isn't marked. The domed face is the kigoroshi-men: literally, the wood-killing face.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Driving a nail, you strike with the flat face, then give the last blows with the domed face, so the surface isn't marked. The domed face is the kee-go-roh-shee men: literally, the wood-killing face.

lines.text: The plane is the kanna. Like the saw, it's pulled toward you. Western and Chinese planes are pushed.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress. Say 'kan-na' with a clear double n, like 'kan' then 'na'.
lines.tts: The plane is the kan-na. Like the saw, it's pulled toward you. Western and Chinese planes are pushed.

lines.text: The blade sits in a wooden block, the dai, usually of oak. In the national skills-test manual, the blade is set by tapping with a hammer: on the blade's head to set it deeper, and on the corners of the block's head end to draw it back.

lines.text: A two-blade plane, nimai-ganna, adds a second iron behind the blade: the chip breaker, uragane. It helps stop tear-out. Like the ryōba, it is a Meiji-era development, not an ancient one.

lines.text: If you work with Western tools, the jobs are the same: bench chisels, a hammer or mallet, a bench plane. The plane is the clearest difference: a Western plane is pushed.

lines.text: Chisels and planes depend on a sharp edge. The skills-test manual warns that a dull tool invites injury, and never to point a chisel's edge at yourself or anyone else. It also says to sharpen chisels and planes well after use.

lines.text: Strike the chisel, or push it. Tap the blade into its block. Pull the plane. And keep every edge sharp.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Say 'nomi' with two short syllables, no long vowel.

lines.text: One note: sharp-tool technique, and how to use these tools safely, is best learned from a teacher, at a bench, in person.
